raw_response:
I'll think this through as the farmer would, then give the plan.

---

Fifty years I have worked this land in Quzhou. The soil here is calcareous fluvo-aquic — good for wheat and maize but needs watching on phosphorus because it ties up in the lime. I read the agricultural bulletins when the village distributes them, and I talk with the input dealer in town. My son works in the city, so it is mostly me and my wife. Labor is the thing I cannot buy back.

My 8 mu: I keep 6 mu in the wheat-maize double crop, and 2 mu in cotton on the sandier corner where the wheat does not do as well. Cotton pays more per mu if the bollworm is controlled, but it demands sprays and hand work. At my age I only keep 2 mu of it.

**Wheat (winter):** Last year I got 480 kg/mu. I will sow an improved variety — Jimai 22 is what most of us plant here, it handles the dry spring. Base fertilizer I apply before sowing: about 40 kg of diammonium phosphate and 15 kg urea, then topdress 15 kg urea at jointing. That gives me around 17 kg N, 8 kg P₂O₅ per mu. Potassium I add 6 kg because the straw returns some back. Four irrigations: before winter, jointing, heading, grain-fill. Two sprays — one for aphids and powdery mildew, one for wheat midge if I see it.

**Maize (summer):** After wheat harvest in June I plant Zhengdan 958 or similar hybrid, no-till into the wheat stubble — saves me the ploughing and holds the moisture. 18 kg N per mu split base and large-trumpet stage, 6 kg P, 6 kg K. One or two irrigations depending on the rain. Two sprays for corn borer and armyworm. I expect 600 kg/mu in a normal year.

**Cotton:** I plant a Bt hybrid — bollworm is not the problem it was twenty years ago because of Bt, but mirid bugs and aphids have taken its place, so I still spray 6 times across the season. Plough the cotton ground because the roots go deep. 14 kg N, 7 kg P, 9 kg K per mu. Three irrigations through the summer. 240 kg/mu of seed cotton is what I aim for.

I would rather spend a few extra yuan on fertilizer than come up short at harvest. That is the lesson of fifty years.
